title: The effect of classroom size and ceiling height on college students' learning performance using virtual reality technology
research_question: This study investigates the effects of classroom size and ceiling height on learning performance using virtual reality technology.

participants.description: College students from Qingdao University of Technology (18 female, 16 male), average age 21.6 years. 76% had normal BMI. Met health criteria (no sensory fever, color blindness, major illnesses), visual acuity 1.0 or higher, <15% prior VR experience.
participants.recruitment: Selected from Qingdao University of Technology

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four virtual classroom settings created in Unity, all 9.0m long. (a) Small and High Room (SHR): 9.0m * 4.5m * 3.9m (40.5 m² area, 3.9m ceiling). (b) Small and Low Room (SLR): 9.0m * 4.5m * 3.0m (40.5 m² area, 3.0m ceiling). (c) Big and Low Room (BLR): 9.0m * 6.9m * 3.9m (62.1 m² area, 3.9m ceiling). (d) Big and High Room (BHR): 9.0m * 6.9m * 4.8m (62.1 m² area, 4.8m ceiling). All models furnished identically.
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Figure 1 and Experiment scene design section

measures.instrument: EEG-Theta and Alpha average power values

mechanisms: Environmental characteristics (room size, ceiling height) influence psychological states (pleasure, relaxation, focus, fatigue).
Psychological states, in turn, modulate cognitive resources and learning performance.
Physiological indicators (HRV-nLF/nHF) reflect mental arousal and attention intensity, which are linked to learning performance.
Neural indicators (EEG-Beta frequency power) reflect cognitive activity and attention intensity, correlating with learning outcomes.
EEG fatigue level reflects mental fatigue, which negatively impacts performance.
Ceiling height affects emotional responses (e.g., 'happy', 'comfortable', 'interesting') and can influence behavior (restrained/focused vs. socially active).
The human body processes external information through the central nervous system, generating behavioral processes influenced by environmental factors.
implementation_implications: Classroom size and ceiling height play a crucial role in learning performance.
Classroom design should consider these factors to enhance learning performance and promote physical and mental well-being among college students.
Optimal learning environments can be developed by considering the interplay of spatial dimensions and their effects on subjective and objective measures.

limitations: The sample population was somewhat limited due to thorough screening, potentially raising the risk of a Type II error (false-negative findings).
Subjective evaluations of pleasure and relaxation were collected only after the task test; future studies should collect them before and after to assess changes.
A 'ceiling effect' was observed in task scores, where many participants scored near-perfect, limiting conclusions about environmental effects.
Other related variables, such as the deployment of personnel (teacher/students) in the virtual environment, were not assessed.

The study was conducted in a virtual environment, and while differences between VR and real environments are minimal, some are inevitable; future research should include comparative studies between virtual and real environments.
The study was unable to identify patterns between various task test types and the presence of an active distribution of EEG-beta power values.

paper_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The effect of classroom size and ceiling height on college students’ learning performance using virtual reality technology
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractThe physical characteristics of classrooms can significantly impact the physical and mental health as well as the learning performance of college students. This study investigates the effects of classroom size and ceiling height on learning performance using virtual reality technology. Four classroom settings were created: two small classrooms (40.5 m2) with ceiling heights of 3.0 m and 3.9 m, and two large classrooms (62.1 m2) with ceiling heights of 3.9 m and 4.8 m. 34 students participated in task tests while their subjective evaluations and physiological data were recorded. Results showed higher subjective ratings in larger classrooms with the same ceiling height. Classroom size did not significantly affect task test scores. However, there is a significant difference in Task test scores for ceilings of different heights with the same size classroom. The task test improved by 17.3% in the Big and High Room (BHR) and by 20.1% in the Small and Low Room (SLR). Physiological data revealed significant effects of ceiling height, with HRV-nLF/nHF and EEG-β power increasing by 26.5% and 53.9% in BHR, and by 10.7% and 22.8% in SLR, respectively. This study concludes that classroom size and ceiling height plays a crucial role in learning performance and provides insights for classroom design. It also establishes a framework for future research on the interplay between heart rate variability, EEG, and learning performance.
